title: “TREAT THEM AS A PAGAN OR TAX COLLECTOR” — DID JESUS REALLY TELL US TO CUT PEOPLE OFF?
paragraphs: “TREAT THEM AS A PAGAN OR TAX COLLECTOR” — DID JESUS REALLY TELL US TO CUT PEOPLE OFF?

One of Jesus’ most misunderstood commands has been used to justify rejection, silence, and spiritual abandonment. But when you discover how Jesus actually treated pagans and tax collectors, His words become both more confronting and more beautiful than you ever imagined.
There is a kind of pain that only another Christian can give you.
Not because unbelievers cannot wound you. They can.

But there is something uniquely devastating about being hurt by someone who knows the same Scriptures you know. Someone who sings about grace on Sunday and then treats you like you are beyond its reach on Monday.
Maybe you have experienced it.
You made a mistake. Perhaps a terrible one.
People found out.
The conversations changed. The invitations stopped. The smiles became uncomfortable. Suddenly, people who once called you brother or sister began treating you like a stranger.
And somewhere in the middle of your shame, somebody opened a Bible and said:
“Well, Jesus told us to treat them like a pagan or a tax collector.”
And just like that, rejection sounded holy.
But what if we have been reading those words without paying attention to the Man who spoke them?
What if the same Jesus who commanded the Church to confront sin also showed us something extraordinary about how to treat sinners?
And what if His command was never permission to become cruel, but a call to take sin seriously without forgetting the heart of God?
Stay with me, because the answer is not as comfortable as either side might hope.
It will challenge those who use grace to excuse unrepentant sin.
And it will confront those who use holiness as an excuse to stop loving people.
Most importantly, it may change the way you see someone you have already decided is beyond restoration.
Jesus said:
“Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.”
— Matthew 18:15, KJV
Read those final words again.
“Thou hast gained thy brother.”
Not, “You have won the argument.”
Not, “You have exposed the sinner.”
Not, “You have proven yourself spiritually superior.”
You have gained your brother.
That is the heartbeat of the passage.
Restoration.
Jesus begins with a person who has sinned and another person who must decide what to do about it.
And His first instruction is surprisingly private.
Go to the person.
Alone.
Before you gather an audience. Before you tell the prayer group every detail. Before you post something mysterious on Facebook that everyone knows is about them.
Go privately.
Why?
Because biblical correction is not supposed to become public humiliation.
Jesus is protecting the possibility of repentance without unnecessary shame.
He is giving the person an opportunity to listen, acknowledge the wrong, and turn back.
In the Greek text, the phrase translated “thou hast gained thy brother” is:
ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου
ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou
Literally, “you have gained your brother.”
The verb kerdainō carries the idea of gaining or winning something.
Jesus describes a restored relationship as a gain.
Think about that.
In a world where people compete to win arguments, Jesus is concerned about winning back a brother.
And notice something else.
Jesus does not say that love means pretending the offense never happened.
He says to confront it.
Because genuine love does not celebrate the destruction of the person it claims to care about.
Sometimes love has to say, “What you did was wrong.”
Sometimes love has to say, “This cannot continue.”
Sometimes love must speak a truth that risks being rejected.
But love never needs to enjoy another person's disgrace.
And this is where the passage becomes difficult.
Jesus continues:
“But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.”
— Matthew 18:16, KJV
If private correction fails, Jesus instructs us to involve one or two others.
Not a mob.
Not an online audience.
Not people recruited to destroy somebody's reputation.
One or two.
The language echoes Deuteronomy 19:15, where multiple witnesses establish a matter.
The principle is serious: accusations must be handled responsibly.
Truth matters.
Evidence matters.
Fairness matters.
The accused person must not be condemned simply because someone tells a persuasive story.
And the person bringing the concern must also be accountable.
That should make every Christian careful.
Because not every accusation is true.
Not every disagreement is sin.
Not every person who questions a leader is rebellious.
And not every person who refuses an unjust demand is refusing to obey Jesus.
Church discipline must never become a weapon for silencing legitimate concerns, protecting abusive leadership, or demanding loyalty to human authority over God's Word.
If someone is being abused, threatened, manipulated, or harmed, Matthew 18 must not be twisted into a requirement that they privately confront a dangerous person or remain in an unsafe situation.
Protecting the vulnerable, seeking appropriate outside help, and reporting criminal conduct to the proper authorities are not betrayals of Christian forgiveness.
They can be expressions of truth, justice, and love.
Jesus did not give His Church permission to hide evil.
He gave His people responsibility to deal truthfully with it.
Then comes the sentence that has troubled believers for generations.
“And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.”
— Matthew 18:17, KJV
There it is.
The phrase that has ended friendships.
The phrase that has been quoted in church meetings.
The phrase that has sometimes been used to justify complete social rejection.
“Let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.”
But before we decide what Jesus meant, we need to understand what His original hearers would have heard.
The Greek reads:
ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης
estō soi hōsper ho ethnikos kai ho telōnēs
A careful translation is:
“Let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector.”
The word ethnikos refers here to someone belonging to the nations outside the Jewish covenant community—a Gentile or outsider.
The word telōnēs refers to a tax collector.
In first-century Jewish society, tax collectors were often despised because of their association with Roman taxation and the opportunities their work created for exploitation and corruption.
For many Jewish listeners, Gentiles and tax collectors represented people outside the recognized religious community.
So Jesus' statement was not a small matter.
He was describing a real change in how an unrepentant person should be regarded within the community of disciples.
But here is the question we cannot afford to ignore.
How did Jesus Himself treat Gentiles and tax collectors?
Because if we interpret His command in a way that contradicts His character, we have probably misunderstood something.
Consider Matthew.
Before Matthew became a disciple, he was a tax collector.
The kind of person religious society often despised.
The kind of person people avoided.
The kind of person whose occupation made him a symbol of compromise and corruption.
And one day, Jesus approached his tax booth.
Imagine Matthew sitting there.
Coins on the table.
People passing by with disgust in their eyes.
Perhaps accustomed to being judged before he even opened his mouth.
Then Jesus looked at him.
And said two words.
Matthew 9:9 records that Matthew arose and followed Him.
Jesus did not pretend Matthew's former life was irrelevant.
He called him into an entirely new life.
But He did not treat Matthew as someone incapable of receiving mercy.
And what happened next?
Jesus sat at a meal with tax collectors and sinners.
The Pharisees were offended.
They asked why He ate with such people.
Jesus answered:
“They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.”
— Matthew 9:12, KJV
Then He said:
“But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
— Matthew 9:13, KJV
Did you catch that?
Mercy. And repentance.
Not mercy instead of repentance.
Not repentance without mercy.
Both.
Jesus welcomed sinners without blessing their sin.
He approached the spiritually sick as a physician, not as someone who enjoyed watching them die.
That changes the conversation.
When Jesus tells His disciples to regard an obstinately unrepentant person as a Gentile or tax collector, He is not commanding them to pretend that person remains in good standing within the Church.
The context requires a genuine boundary.
But neither does the wider Gospel permit us to interpret that boundary as permission for hatred, humiliation, revenge, or indifference.
Jesus treated outsiders as people who needed truth, repentance, and the invitation of grace.
The Church must never confuse removing the recognition of fellowship with removing the obligation to love.
Those are not the same thing.
And we must be careful here.
Some people read Matthew 18 and conclude that Jesus was simply saying, “Keep treating them exactly as before.”
But that does not adequately account for the escalating process He described.
Private correction failed.
Witnesses were involved.
The matter was brought before the church.
The person still refused to listen.
Jesus was describing a serious rupture in recognized fellowship.
The New Testament confirms that church discipline can involve the removal of an unrepentant person from the community's fellowship.
In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul addresses a scandalous situation of sexual immorality being tolerated within the Corinthian church.
He does not tell the believers to celebrate their tolerance.
He calls them to act.
In verse 5, he describes a severe disciplinary action with a redemptive purpose:
“That the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”
Even there, the stated ultimate concern is salvation.
Not entertainment.
Not humiliation.
Not revenge.
And Paul distinguishes between judging those who profess to belong to the Church and judging outsiders.
In 1 Corinthians 5:12–13, he makes clear that the Church has a responsibility to address serious sin within its own fellowship.
This is not a license to police the entire world.
It is a call for integrity among those who claim to follow Christ.
But the story does not end with exclusion.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks about a disciplined individual who should now be forgiven, comforted, and reassured of love, lest he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
We should not automatically assume that this is the same individual described in 1 Corinthians 5; scholars differ on that identification.
Nevertheless, the passage reveals an essential apostolic principle.
Discipline must not become permanent punishment when repentance and restoration are appropriate.
Paul says:
“Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him.”
— 2 Corinthians 2:8, KJV
Confirm your love.
Not merely tolerate his presence.
Not keep reminding him of the worst thing he ever did.
Confirm your love.
Can you imagine how different some churches would be if they took both sides of Scripture seriously?
What if we stopped calling everything grace when we are actually afraid to confront sin?
And what if we stopped calling everything holiness when we are actually enjoying someone's downfall?
Because there are two dangerous distortions of the Gospel.
One says, “God loves you, so repentance does not matter.”
The other says, “You sinned, so God's people should never love you again.”
Neither reflects the fullness of Jesus Christ.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
And holiness is not permission to become heartless.
Now think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.

The account appears in John 7:53–8:11 in many Bibles, though responsible study must acknowledge that the passage is absent from the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John and is marked as textually disputed in many modern translations.
That textual issue matters.
We should never conceal it when claiming to handle Scripture faithfully.
The account nevertheless reflects a pattern consistent with the mercy and moral seriousness seen elsewhere in Jesus' ministry.
The accusers wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy.
And the woman heard words that hold mercy and moral transformation together:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11, KJV
Do not miss either half.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
And:
“Sin no more.”
Some of us want the first sentence without the second.
Others seem to love the second sentence while forgetting the first.
But Jesus speaks both.
And the Gospel is diminished whenever we separate what Christ holds together.
Now perhaps you are reading this as someone who has been disciplined, rejected, or publicly shamed.
Perhaps you genuinely sinned.
Perhaps you hurt someone.
Perhaps you lied, betrayed trust, fell into sexual sin, became consumed by pride, or allowed a hidden habit to grow until it damaged your life.
And maybe you have spent years convincing yourself that because people stopped believing in you, God must have stopped calling you.
Listen carefully.
Human rejection is not proof that divine mercy has run out.
But neither is divine mercy an excuse to avoid accountability.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have harmed someone, acknowledge the harm.
Where restitution is possible and appropriate, pursue it.
If trust has been broken, understand that rebuilding it may take time.
And if the person you harmed needs distance or protection, respect that boundary.
Forgiveness does not automatically erase consequences.
Repentance does not entitle anyone to immediate access to another person's life.
Reconciliation, especially after serious harm, may require safety, time, demonstrated change, and the willing participation of those involved.
But hear this:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There was another disciple whose failure became painfully public.
Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted that even if others abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Then the pressure came.
The questions.
The fear.
The danger of being associated with a condemned Man.
And Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of the One he loved.
The memory of his promises.
The crushing realization of what he had done.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Have you ever cried because you finally understood what your sin had cost?
Not because you were caught.
Not because your reputation suffered.
But because you realized you had grieved the One who loved you?
Peter knew that kind of sorrow.
And after the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, Jesus questioned Peter three times about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of restoration.
But notice what restoration involved.
Peter was not simply told to forget the past.
He was called again to love Christ and serve His people.
Grace did not leave Peter where failure had found him.
Grace brought him into renewed obedience.
That is what Jesus does.
And perhaps that is why the phrase “tax collector” carries such extraordinary meaning when we read it through the whole Gospel.
Because Matthew was a tax collector.
And Jesus called him.
Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector.
And Jesus entered his house.
In Luke 19, Zacchaeus responded with a commitment to generosity and restitution.
Jesus declared:
“This day is salvation come to this house.”
— Luke 19:9, KJV
Then He explained His mission:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
— Luke 19:10, KJV
Seek.
And save.
Not seek and shame.
Not seek and exploit.
Not seek and publicly destroy.
Seek and save.
But notice that Zacchaeus' encounter with Jesus produced visible change.
The Gospel did not merely comfort his conscience.
It transformed his relationship with money, wrongdoing, and his neighbors.
This is the kind of grace that rewrites lives.
Not cheap grace that leaves sin untouched.
Not harsh religion that leaves wounded people without hope.
The grace of Jesus Christ that forgives, confronts, restores, and transforms.
And this brings us back to Matthew 18.
Because there is something remarkable about the surrounding context.
Before Jesus gives instructions about confronting a sinning brother, He tells the parable of the lost sheep.
In Matthew 18:12–14, the shepherd seeks the one sheep that has gone astray.
And Jesus concludes:
“Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.”
— Matthew 18:14, KJV
Immediately afterward comes the instruction to confront a sinning brother.
That literary context matters.
Jesus is not suddenly changing from a Shepherd who seeks the lost into a religious official who enjoys expelling people.
The concern for those who wander helps us understand the purpose of correction.
And immediately after the teaching on church discipline, Peter asks how often he must forgive his brother.
Seven times?
Jesus responds:
“I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.”
— Matthew 18:22, KJV
The expression communicates forgiveness that is not governed by a petty numerical limit.
So look at the movement of the chapter.
A sheep wanders.
A brother sins.
A community must respond.
And forgiveness remains central.
This does not cancel the need for boundaries.
It explains the heart with which boundaries should be maintained.
The Church must be holy.
But it must also remember whose Church it is.
We belong to the One who carried a cross for sinners.
And there is another Greek word worth considering.
In Matthew 18:15, Jesus uses the word:
ἁμαρτήσῃ
hamartēsē
A form of the verb hamartanō, meaning “to sin.”
Jesus is addressing sin, not simply an unpleasant personality, a disagreement over preferences, or a person's failure to satisfy our expectations.
That distinction is crucial.
Church discipline must not become a method for punishing people who disagree with leadership about nonessential matters.
Nor should Christians confuse personal offense with demonstrated wrongdoing.

Some ancient manuscripts of Matthew 18:15 include the words “against you,” while others do not. That textual variation affects whether the opening statement is understood specifically as a personal offense or more broadly as a brother's sin.
Either way, the passage calls for truthful, proportionate, and restorative action—not impulsive condemnation.
And now we must face an uncomfortable question.
What if you are not the wounded person in this story?
What if you are the one holding the stone?
What if someone sinned years ago, repented, sought help, and began rebuilding their life, but you still introduce them by what they used to be?
What if you say you believe in the transforming power of Christ but refuse to believe that Christ can transform someone you personally dislike?
What if you have been calling bitterness discernment?
What if you have been calling gossip a prayer request?
What if you have been calling humiliation accountability?
That is a painful question.
Because sometimes the person most resistant to grace is not the sinner who needs correction.
Sometimes it is the religious person who cannot bear to see mercy extended.
Think about the older brother in Luke 15.
The younger son had wasted his inheritance in reckless living.
He returned broken.
His father welcomed him.
But the older brother became angry.
He could not celebrate the restoration of someone whose failure he remembered so clearly.
He had stayed.
He had worked.
He had obeyed.
And now the one who had disgraced the family was being welcomed home.
His resentment revealed something sobering.
It is possible to remain close to the father's house while being far from the father's heart.
The father did not deny the younger son's wrongdoing.
He celebrated his return.
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
— Luke 15:24, KJV
That is the sound of restoration.
And it should make us examine our hearts.
When someone genuinely repents, are we glad?
Or are we disappointed that their story did not end in disgrace?
Do we want people to become holy?
Or do we secretly want them to remain permanently identified by the sin that once made us feel superior?
Jesus did not die so that forgiven sinners could build little kingdoms of condemnation.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
And that reconciliation cost more than any of us could ever pay.
The cross is where this entire conversation must lead.
Because the deepest scandal of Christianity is not that sinners are confronted.
It is that the sinless Son of God willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Jesus was rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And the One who had no sin gave Himself for those who did.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5, KJV
The Hebrew word translated “transgressions” is:
פְּשָׁעֵנוּ
peshaʿenu
“Our transgressions.”
It speaks of our rebellious wrongs.
Not merely unfortunate mistakes.
Not merely imperfections.
Our transgressions.
The Hebrew phrase translated “our iniquities” is:
עֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
ʿavonotenu
Our iniquities—our guilt and moral wrongdoing.
Isaiah does not minimize sin.
He magnifies the astonishing reality of the Servant's suffering on behalf of sinners.
And the New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the suffering Servant's saving work, as seen, for example, in Acts 8:32–35 and 1 Peter 2:24.
That is why Christians cannot afford to become casual about sin.
Sin is serious enough that Christ suffered and died to save us.
But that is also why Christians cannot afford to become casual about mercy.
Grace is precious because of what it cost Him.
At Calvary, God's holiness and His saving love are not competing truths.
They meet in Jesus Christ.
And no one who truly understands the cross should be eager to make another person's shame into entertainment.
Now consider what Paul writes in Galatians 6:1:
The Greek verb translated “restore” is:
καταρτίζετε
katartizete
From katartizō, meaning to restore, put in order, or make fit.
The word can be used for repairing or preparing something so it can serve its intended purpose.
Paul's instruction is not to destroy the fallen person.
It is to seek restoration with gentleness.
And then he adds a warning.
Consider yourself.
Why?
Because the person correcting someone else is not immune to temptation.
Today you may be helping someone stand.
Tomorrow you may desperately need someone to help you.
That is not an argument against correction.
It is an argument for humility.
A mature Christian can confront sin without forgetting their own dependence on grace.
And perhaps that is what we need to recover.
Churches where truth is not sacrificed for popularity.
Where victims are protected.
Where allegations are examined fairly.
Where serious wrongdoing has real consequences.
Where repentance is more than a public apology.
Where leaders are accountable.
Where discipline is never confused with cruelty.
And where genuinely repentant people are not treated as permanently beyond the possibility of spiritual restoration.
Because the Church is not a museum of flawless people.
It is a community called to holiness by a Savior who rescues sinners.
That does not mean everyone who claims to be repentant is safe to trust.
Words alone do not prove transformation.
Jesus Himself taught that people are known by their fruits (Matthew 7:16–20).
A person may say, “I am sorry,” while continuing to manipulate, deceive, exploit, or harm others.
Biblical restoration must not ignore patterns of behavior.
And reconciliation is not always possible, even where forgiveness is sincerely offered.
Some relationships require permanent protective boundaries.
But no boundary requires hatred.
No act of accountability requires cruelty.
And no Christian should confuse someone's exclusion from fellowship with a declaration that God is powerless to save them.
That final judgment belongs to God.
Our responsibility is to be faithful.
Faithful to truth.
Faithful to holiness.
Faithful to justice.
Faithful to mercy.
Faithful to Jesus.
So when someone asks, “Did Jesus really say to treat them as a pagan or tax collector?” the answer is yes.
He did.
And we should not soften His words until they mean nothing.
He taught that persistent, unrepentant sin among professing believers can require a serious change in recognized fellowship.

But when we ask what kind of heart should govern that response, we must look at the same Jesus who called Matthew, sought Zacchaeus, restored Peter, welcomed repentant sinners, and died for the ungodly.
Treating someone as an outsider to the Church's fellowship does not mean treating them as an outsider to the reach of Christian love.
That is the distinction.
Do not affirm what God calls sin.
Do not pretend repentance is unnecessary.
Do not compromise truth to keep the peace.
But do not close your heart to the possibility that the person who has fallen may one day rise by the grace of God.
And if they genuinely repent, do not make your pride an obstacle to the mercy Christ has commanded His people to show.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying the shame of your own failure.
Maybe the church doors still open for everyone else, but you feel too ashamed to walk through them.
Maybe your family knows what happened.
Maybe your children saw you fall.
Maybe your marriage was wounded.
Maybe your testimony became a warning story.
Maybe you have spent years thinking, “If people really knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way.”
But Jesus already knows.
He knows the truth without needing a rumor.
He sees the heart without needing an audience.
He knows the sin you confessed and the sin you are still trying to hide.
And His call is not, “Keep pretending.”
His call is to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is:
μετανοεῖτε
metanoeite
From metanoeō, meaning to repent—to change one's mind and direction in response to God's truth.
Biblical repentance is more than a passing emotion.
It involves a genuine turning from sin toward God, with a changed life bearing fruit consistent with that turning.
You do not have to manufacture a flawless past.
You cannot.
You do not have to convince God that your sin was harmless.
It was not.
You are called to come to Christ in truth.
And if you belong to Him, His grace is not merely a covering for your reputation.
It is the power of God at work in a life being transformed.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not faithful and just to humiliate us forever.
Faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Because forgiveness is grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And if you are the person who has been wronged, perhaps your next step is different.
Maybe you need to stop carrying vengeance.
Maybe you need to forgive without denying what happened.
Maybe you need to maintain a necessary boundary without wishing destruction upon the person who harmed you.
Maybe you need to acknowledge that forgiveness and restored trust are not identical.
You can entrust justice to God while still pursuing appropriate accountability.
You can release personal vengeance without returning to an unsafe relationship.
You can pray for someone's repentance without granting them access to harm you again.
That, too, can be a faithful response to Jesus.
And if you are a pastor, elder, ministry leader, or someone responsible for confronting wrongdoing, remember this:
You are dealing with people for whom Christ died.
Do not trivialize their sin.
Do not trivialize their dignity.
Do not sacrifice the vulnerable to protect an institution.
Do not allow a person's influence, money, popularity, or position to exempt them from accountability.
And do not make discipline a performance designed to demonstrate your authority.
The authority belongs to Christ.
The Church is His.
The sheep are His.
The truth is His.
And the grace is His.
Perhaps this article has brought someone's face to your mind.
Someone who walked away.
Someone who fell.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone your church no longer knows how to approach.
Or perhaps the face you see is your own.
If that is you, I want to ask something deeper than whether you agree with this article.
What is Jesus asking you to do with the truth you have just heard?
To repent?
To forgive?
To seek wise counsel?
To tell the truth?
To stop gossiping?
To protect someone who is being harmed?
To take responsibility for something you have spent years excusing?
To reach out appropriately to someone who is isolated and hurting?
To stop using another person's past as a permanent identity?
Whatever it is, do not let this become another Christian message that moves you emotionally but leaves your life unchanged.
The Word of God is not given merely to make us feel something.
It calls us to respond.
And maybe someone else desperately needs to read this.
Someone who believes their failure disqualified them forever.
Someone who thinks accountability means God has abandoned them.
Someone who has been using Scripture to justify bitterness.
Someone who has confused acceptance with approval.
Someone who is one painful experience away from walking away from the Church entirely.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because truth worth receiving is also worth passing on.
A simple share could help someone reconsider how they understand repentance, church discipline, forgiveness, and the heart of Jesus.
And please, do not leave without joining this conversation.
Or have you witnessed biblical correction lead to genuine repentance and restoration?
You do not need to reveal anyone's private story.
You can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me,” if you are learning what grace and repentance truly mean.
Or comment, “Pray for me,” if you are trying to find your way back to God after a painful season.
We want this to be more than a comment section filled with religious slogans.
We want it to be a place where believers can speak truthfully, encourage one another, and point each other back to Jesus.
There may come a day when you are the one who needs to remember the difference between biblical discipline and religious rejection.
Or when someone you love falls, and you need to remember that truth and compassion are not enemies.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to stay connected.
Bring your family, your friends, the believer struggling quietly, the Christian who has grown spiritually cold, and even the seeker who is still trying to understand who Jesus really is.
We want people to encounter Scripture that does more than inspire them for a moment.
We want them to know Christ, understand His Word, repent of sin, grow in faith, and experience the transforming power of His Gospel.
Not because financial support makes someone a better Christian.
And certainly not because the grace of Jesus Christ can be bought.
It never could be.
Salvation is God's gift, received by grace through faith, not earned through financial contributions or religious works (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), and he commended generous giving that comes from a willing heart rather than pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
It should never be represented as a mandatory biblical tithe, a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church, or a condition for God's blessing.
Rather, it is an opportunity to help sustain and expand this work, so more people can encounter Scripture, receive encouragement, be challenged toward repentance, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
If these messages have helped you, perhaps you can help make it possible for someone else to receive them.
These are expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards.
The greater purpose remains the same: to keep pointing people to Christ.
That free library is part of the mission, too.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep sharing the Gospel.
Because the goal is not merely to build a larger audience.
It is to help people meet the Savior who changes lives.
The same Jesus who called Matthew out of his tax booth.
The same Jesus who brought salvation to Zacchaeus' house.
The same Jesus who restored Peter after his denial.
The same Jesus who commanded His Church to confront sin and taught His disciples to forgive.
The same Jesus who went to the cross, rose from the grave, and still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
So the next time you hear someone quote, “Treat them as a pagan or tax collector,” remember the whole counsel of Scripture.
Remember the necessary seriousness of church discipline.
Remember the dignity of people made in God's image.
Remember that repentance matters.
Remember that accountability matters.
Remember that protecting the vulnerable matters.
And remember how Jesus treated the people religious society considered hopeless.
He did not affirm their sin.
He called them to Himself.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not need to rewrite history to redeem a human life.
He tells the truth about our sin.
He bears the cost of our salvation.
He calls us to repentance.
And He gives us a future that our past could never have earned.
So do not use the Bible to excuse the sin Jesus came to save us from.
And do not use the Bible to deny the mercy Jesus died to give.
Because one day, the person standing in need of correction, forgiveness, patience, and restoration may be you.
And on that day, you will understand why the Church must never choose between truth and love.
Christ commands us to walk in both.
Never forget: the hands that were pierced for sinners are the same hands calling the fallen to rise, the wandering to return, and the forgiven to become new.
